source.title: LangFIR: Discovering Sparse Language-Specific Features from Monolingual Data for Language Steering
source.authors: S. Wong; Hassan Sajjad; A. Siddique

record.tranche_reason: Tests sparse SAE-recoverable language features in multilingual LLMs, a new setting relative to toy-model superposition; it does not test the original toy-model geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports sample-size and threshold stability, feature counts and selectivity, layer-wise feature analyses, and directional-ablation effects. Steering benchmark scores and other method comparisons are not included as rows because they measure generation-control performance rather than the representational claims.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper (LangFIR). It uses pretrained SAEs (Llama Scope, Gemma Scope 2) as a tool to pick language-specific features, then reports how well those features steer output language. Superposition is cited only to explain why neuron-based methods are unreliable. The representational analyses (Sec. 5) validate the method's own selected features: selectivity and ablation effects on chosen SAE latents. They do not test whether models store features in superposition or whether an SAE recovers them. They also do not test whether SAE features are complete, canonical or stable across dictionaries. The record's T3/'tests' guess is not supported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that random-token filtering with only monolingual data finds sparse, language-selective, causally relevant SAE features concentrated in later layers. They also report that steering vectors built from these features give the best average ACC×BLEU among steering methods across three models, three datasets and 12 languages, while Prompt Only scores higher on the translation task. They note that English is an exception, and that larger models, balanced-language models and low-resource languages remain open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained SAEs, random-token filtering, and multilingual-LM feature ablation/steering; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method or measure its geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature counts stabilize for τ ≥ 0.8, with very high thresholds potentially excluding weaker features; identified feature counts and feature activation magnitudes vary by layer, with stronger activations in later layers. Sample-size results stabilize by around 100 sentences. English is an exception in activation and ablation effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Few language-selective SAE latents pass the filter: under 5 per language in Llama 3.1 8B (Fig. 2b). These are near-zero on other languages (Fig. 3b), and ablating the top-2 raises cross-entropy only for the target language (Figs. 4, 11). English is the exception (near-zero activation and ablation effect).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language identity in multilingual LLMs is concentrated in a few sparse SAE feature directions, with English less separable (possibly entangled with general concepts).

record.problems: Representational analyses focus primarily on Llama 3.1 8B and five languages; English is a notable exception to the reported causal effects. The authors limit evaluation to three models under 10B parameters from two English-centric families and mostly mid- to high-resource languages. Several ablation and layer-wise values are presented only in figures, without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, or geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
No analysis of the origins of polysemanticity.
Does not test whether features are spread across neurons. Does not test whether SAEs recover sparse features beyond using off-the-shelf SAEs as a tool.
No test of completeness, canonicality, or stability across SAE widths, seeds or training choices. The sample-size and τ stability concerns the method's own selection.
Treats decoder columns as 1-D directions by assumption; no comparison with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition appears only as a citation (Elhage et al. 2022) motivating SAEs over neurons. All representational analyses are on Llama 3.1 8B with the Llama Scope 8x SAE. Steering results and benchmark comparisons are method performance and were correctly excluded. Consider reclassifying this study out of the superposition test set.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, overlap geometry, near-orthogonality, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether features compete for limited capacity, nor whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE-identified sparse language features in three LLMs, with most representational analyses on Llama 3.1 8B. Does not test whether features are spread across many neurons.
Tests sample-size/threshold stability and causal effects for identified SAE features, but not completeness, canonicality, or stability across different SAE dictionaries or training choices.
Uses decoder columns as individual feature directions but does not compare 1-D directions against multidimensional features or test superposition geometry.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured overlap of language-consistent and random-token language-agnostic SAE feature sets across sample sizes.

conditions.value: sweep; exact values not stated in prose

rows.value: Overlap approaches 100%; both sets stabilize by around 100 sentences.
rows.note: The result is described in the text; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Selection value of the paper's own filtering step (overlap between language-consistent and random-token feature sets). It measures how many candidates the method discards, not superposition or SAE canonicality.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Counted language-specific features remaining after random-token overlap removal across sample sizes.

conditions.value: sweep; exact values not stated in prose

rows.value: Typically fewer than five per language; counts stabilize by around 100 sentences.
rows.note: The paper reports sparse residual feature sets and sample-size stability; it does not give exact counts in prose.
rows.check: Selection value: how many features survive the method's filter, and how this varies with sample size. This is the method's convergence, not stability of SAE features as model units across dictionaries.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Varied the activation-frequency threshold used to identify language-specific SAE features.
rows.measure: Feature count stability across frequency thresholds
rows.value: Feature counts stabilize for τ ≥ 0.8; very high thresholds may exclude weaker language-specific features.
rows.note: The reported threshold robustness has a stated qualification at very high thresholds.
rows.check: Sensitivity of the method's selection to its own hyperparameter τ; not a V5 stability test. The 'partial' state has no meaning against any version.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean activation magnitudes of identified language-specific features.
rows.measure: Mean activation magnitude by feature rank
rows.value: For all non-English languages, the rank-1 feature dominates in mean activation magnitude; English is the exception, with its rank-1 feature activating at near-zero magnitude.
rows.note: The paper describes the qualitative pattern; values in the plotted figure are not transcribed here.
rows.check: Describes activation magnitudes of the method's selected features. The rank-1 feature dominates for the 4 non-English languages; English's rank-1 is near zero. This bears on language localization, not on a superposition version. 'Partial' was relative to no version.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured each language's rank-1 identified feature on texts in the five evaluation languages.

conditions.value: rank-1 language-specific feature for each of English, Portuguese, German, Polish, Chinese
five languages: English, Portuguese, German, Polish, Chinese

rows.measure: Mean SAE feature activation by evaluation language
rows.baseline: Near-zero activation on non-target languages, as described by the authors.
rows.value: Each feature activates strongly only on its corresponding target language and is near zero for the others.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative description across the five target features; individual matrix values are not assigned because the flattened layout is ambiguous.
rows.check: Rank-1 features are language-selective, e.g. PT 7.28 vs 0.00 elsewhere (Fig. 3b). This validates the selected features; it is not a test of superposition or SAE recoverability as such.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Counted identified language-specific features across model layers.
rows.value: Counts peak at the earliest and latest layers, dip in middle layers, and recover in later layers.
rows.note: The text gives the layer-wise pattern, not exact plotted counts.
rows.check: Layer-wise count of selected features; descriptive. No version predicts this pattern, so 'partial' is meaningless.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean activation magnitude of language-specific features across layers.
rows.value: Late-layer features activate more strongly than early-layer ones; activation magnitudes peak in later layers.
rows.note: The authors describe stronger later-layer activation; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Layer-wise activation magnitude of selected features; descriptive and unrelated to any version.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B
rows.operation_detail: Directionally ablated the top-2 identified language-specific features per layer and measured cross-entropy change.
rows.baseline: Other-language texts show negligible effects, as described by the authors.

rows.note: No exact plotted values are stated; the text describes the target-selective effect.
rows.check: Ablation validates the causal role of the method's selected Portuguese features (Fig. 4a). It bears on language localization, not on a version.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama 3.1 8B; identified language-specific SAE features across the five analyzed languages
reader_labels.reason: The paper identifies very sparse feature sets, reports language-selective activation, and finds target-selective loss increases under ablation for non-English targets (R2, R5, R8, R9, R11, R12). This supports the SAE-recoverable-feature part of V4, not its neuron-distribution alternative.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: English's rank-1 feature activates at near-zero magnitude and ablating identified English features produces near-zero CE change across most layers (R4, R10).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Identified features in Llama 3.1 8B under sample-size and threshold variation; non-English causal ablation tests
reader_labels.reason: Feature counts stabilize by around 100 samples and for τ ≥ 0.8, and identified non-English features have selective activation and target-specific ablation effects (R2, R3, R5, R8, R9, R11, R12). These findings support tested stability and functional relevance only, not completeness or canonicality.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: English identified features show near-zero rank-1 activation and little CE change on ablation, limiting the claim that the identified features function as complete units for every tested language (R4, R10).
